options: A table that maps a name to the information needed to find a file
The raw bytes of every file concatenated
A CPU register
An interrupt vector
questions.explanation: The directory answers “what does this name mean?”. The file’s bytes live in data blocks found from that answer.

questions.prompt: In a Unix-style file system, the file’s name lives
options: In the directory entry, while the inode stores metadata and block pointers
Only inside the inode, and the directory stores the file’s bytes
In the program counter
In the TLB
questions.explanation: Several names can point at one inode (hard links). That only works if the name stays in the directory and the inode stays nameless.
traps: Putting the filename inside the inode.

questions.prompt: Contiguous allocation gives fast sequential reads and
options: Makes a file hard to grow when the next blocks are already taken
Removes any need to track free space
Places every block at a random offset with no record
Forbids directories
questions.explanation: One extent is easy to read. Growing it needs a free neighbor, or a copy to a larger hole.

options: Lets a file use any free blocks, but random access walks the chain
Requires one huge contiguous run
Stores no pointers at all
Cannot represent a file larger than one block
questions.explanation: Each block points at the next. There is no external fragmentation. Reaching block n costs n steps unless you add an index.

questions.prompt: An index block, or an inode’s pointer array, helps because
options: Block n of a file can be found without reading the previous data blocks
The file must be contiguous
Directories become unnecessary
Free space can be ignored
questions.explanation: The index is a table of block addresses. One read of the index, plus one read of the data block, reaches an arbitrary offset.

questions.prompt: Which statements about allocating file blocks are true?
options: A free-space bitmap uses one bit per block to say whether that block is free
Contiguous allocation can make a file hard to grow
An index lets you find block n without reading every earlier data block
The directory entry stores the raw bytes of the file
questions.explanation: A bitmap tracks free blocks. Contiguous files need a larger hole to grow. An index is a table of block addresses. The directory maps a name; it does not hold the file’s bytes.
traps: The file’s bytes live in data blocks, not in the name.

questions.prompt: A journaling file system writes intended metadata changes to a log so that
options: After a crash it can finish or undo a partial update
Files never occupy blocks
The CPU can skip interrupts
Directories live in registers
questions.explanation: The log makes an update atomic from the recovery program’s point of view. Without it, a crash can leave a pointer to a block that was never claimed, or the reverse.

options: Starts at the root and does not depend on the current directory
Is always shorter than a relative path
Contains only an inode number and no names
Cannot name a directory
questions.explanation: A relative path is resolved from the current directory. An absolute path names every step from the root.

questions.prompt: Why can removing a name from a directory leave the file’s bytes on disk?
questions.answer: Another name may still point at the same inode, or a process may still have the file open.
questions.explanation: The bytes are reclaimed when the link count and the open count both hit zero. “Delete” often just drops a directory entry.
